claims.claim: A single life given wholly to God is a higher calling than marriage.
Marrying again after your spouse has died is perfectly fine.

stances.summary: Marriage is good, but its best fruit is that it produces virgins. Virginity stands above marriage as gold stands above silver.
stances.quote: I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in Rome in 384 to the young consecrated virgin Eustochium. Jerome pressed the point hardest in Against Jovinian (393), book 1, section 3: "while we honour marriage we prefer virginity which is the offspring of marriage", and in section 7 he argued that if it is good not to touch a woman, it is bad to touch one. Section 16 of the same book has "Marriage replenishes the earth, virginity fills Paradise." Friends in Rome thought he had gone too far. In Letter 48 to Pammachius he defended himself and insisted he did not condemn marriage. He never changed his ranking. Orthodox; a Doctor of the Church in the West.

stances.summary: Marrying is no sin, and he does not discourage it. But marriage is a remedy for weakness, while virginity wins glory, so virginity is the higher of two good things.
stances.quote: The one sins not if she marries, the other, if she marries not, it is for eternity. In the former is the remedy for weakness, in the latter the glory of chastity. The former is not reproved, the latter is praised.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF second series vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written in 377, early in his time as bishop, for his sister Marcellina, a consecrated virgin. The same chapter opens: "I am not indeed discouraging marriage, but am enlarging upon the benefits of virginity." In section 35 he adds: "I am comparing good things with good things, that it may be clear which is the more excellent." In section 58 he admits that many virgins who wanted to follow his teaching were held back by their mothers. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: Marriage is a real good, not just a lesser evil than fornication. But marriage and continence are two goods, and continence is the better one.
stances.quote: Therefore marriage and fornication are not two evils, whereof the second is worse: but marriage and continence are two goods, whereof the second is better
stances.translation: C.L. Cornish, NPNF first series vol. 3, 1887
stances.work: On the Good of Marriage (De bono coniugali)
stances.context: Written about 401, partly to answer Jovinian, who said marriage and virginity were of equal merit. Augustine defends marriage against those who despised it and defends the rank of virginity against Jovinian. In On Holy Virginity he adds a strong warning against pride: a virgin should hold "that the virginal good is much greater and better than the married good" while not knowing "whether this or that married woman be not already able to suffer for Christ, but herself as yet unable" (section 47 in NPNF). His own life: he lived with a partner for about fifteen years, then chose continence at his conversion in 386. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: The unmarried life is higher. Yet a couple who marry with the right aims fall only a little short of the monks.
stances.quote: If any marry thus, with these views, he will be but little inferior to monks; the married but little below the unmarried.
stances.translation: Gross Alexander, NPNF first series vol. 13, 1889
stances.context: Preached in Antioch as a priest (386-398). As a young man he lived as a monk and then a hermit near Antioch, and he wrote a whole treatise On Virginity (about 382) arguing that virginity is superior. Its only English versions are modern and copyrighted, so it is not quoted here; its line "Whoever denigrates marriage also diminishes the glory of virginity" is quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1620. In Homily 19 on 1 Corinthians he says Paul "signifies that continence is better, and yet puts no force on the person who cannot attain to it". As a preacher he increasingly urged married lay people toward the same seriousness as monks, and this homily shows that warmer view of marriage. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Virginity is the better way. He writes as a married man who regrets that the door to it is now closed to him.
stances.quote: Happy they who have still the power of choosing the better way, and have not debarred themselves from it by engagements of the secular life, as we have, whom a gulf now divides from glorious virginity
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Written about 371, at the request of his brother Basil. This chapter is the main evidence that Gregory himself was married. He is careful not to condemn marriage: chapter 8 begins "Let no one think however that herein we depreciate marriage as an institution. We are well aware that it is not a stranger to God's blessing." Orthodox.

stances.summary: Marriage is honourable, but virginity is higher. Virginity would be no great thing if it were not better than a good thing.
stances.quote: Marriage is honourable; but I cannot say that it is more lofty than virginity; for virginity were no great thing if it were not better than a good thing.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached in Constantinople in 380. He immediately softens it: "Do not however be angry, you women that are subject to the yoke... be bound together, both virgins and wives, and be one in the Lord, and each others' adornment." He adds that there would be no celibate if there were no marriage. His own father was a married bishop. Orthodox.

stances.summary: There are two ways of life. Marriage is the ordinary way and is blameless. Virginity is the angelic way and wins greater gifts.
stances.quote: For there are two ways in life, as touching these matters. The one the more moderate and ordinary, I mean marriage; the other angelic and unsurpassed, namely virginity. Now if a man choose the way of the world, namely marriage, he is not indeed to blame; yet he will not receive such great gifts as the other.
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written to the monk Amun, who was troubled by questions of bodily purity. In the same passage Athanasius insists the body is not unclean and says "He is blessed who, being freely yoked in his youth, naturally begets children." He ranks the married thirtyfold and the virgin hundredfold. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Consecrated virginity outranks widowhood and marriage. A virgin is the bride of Christ.
stances.quote: Widowhood is inferior to virginity; consequently the sin of the widows comes far behind that of the virgins.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Letter 199, the second canonical letter to Amphilochius
stances.context: Written about 375. The line comes in a rule about penalties for consecrated virgins who break their vow, so it states a ranking in passing rather than arguing it. Basil organised ascetic communities and his rules assume that the celibate life is the fuller form of discipleship. No blunt comparison of marriage and celibacy was found in his public-domain English works. Orthodox.

stances.summary: God first commanded people to multiply, then invited some to continence. Those who give up the desires of the flesh are seeking the better dwellings in heaven.
stances.quote: But when He says that in His Father's house are many mansions, He points out the dwellings of the better habitation. Those better habitations you are seeking; cutting away the desires of the flesh, you obtain the reward of a greater grace in the heavenly home.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: On the Dress of Virgins (De habitu virginum)
stances.context: Written about 249, early in his time as bishop. The section opens: "The first decree commanded to increase and to multiply; the second enjoined continency." He adds that the Lord does not command this but exhorts it, "since the free choice of the will is left." In section 3 he calls virgins "the more illustrious portion of Christ's flock." Martyred 258. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Chastity has three ranks: virgins first, the continent second, married people third. All three are glorious.
stances.quote: But chastity maintains the first rank in virgins, the second in those who are continent, the third in the case of wedlock. Yet in all it is glorious, with all its degrees.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886 (printed as "Of the Discipline and Advantage of Chastity", among works once credited to Cyprian)
stances.work: On the Good of Chastity (De bono pudicitiae)
stances.context: ANF printed this among treatises wrongly credited to Cyprian. Modern scholars assign it to Novatian, who wrote it as a letter to his people while absent, after 251. Section 7 goes further: "virginity places itself on an equality with angels; moreover, if we investigate, it even excels them" Novatian led a rigorist schism at Rome from 251 and died about 258 (the date is uncertain). He was orthodox on the Trinity but schismatic. Later Novatianists refused communion to the twice-married (see notes), but no surviving text of Novatian himself says so.

stances.summary: Paul allows marriage only as better than burning with desire. A good praised only by comparison with an evil is a small good. Better still is neither to marry nor to burn.
stances.quote: In fact, in that it is written, To marry is better than to burn, what, pray, is the nature of this good which is (only) commended by comparison with evil, so that the reason why marrying is more good is (merely) that burning is less? Nay, but how far better is it neither to marry nor to burn?
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 200-206, before his Montanist turn, to his own wife, since he was married. The same chapter says "What is permitted is not good" in an analogy with fleeing persecution. He says plainly that he does not forbid marriage and attacks those who do. In his later Montanist period (from about 207) he grew harsher (see claim b). Heterodox in his later years: he joined the Montanist New Prophecy.

stances.summary: Virginity is the best and noblest way of life, the root and first flower of immortality.
stances.quote: Virginity is something supernaturally great, wonderful, and glorious; and, to speak plainly and in accordance with the Holy Scriptures, this best and noblest manner of life alone is the root of immortality, and also its flower and first-fruits
stances.translation: William R. Clark, ANF vol. 6, 1886
stances.work: The Banquet of the Ten Virgins (Symposium)
stances.context: Methodius (died about 311) wrote a dialogue in the style of Plato in which ten virgins each give a speech in praise of virginity. The words belong to the character Marcella, but the whole work argues Methodius's own thesis. Discourse 2 (Theophila) defends marriage and childbearing as still good. Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: The highest blessing is virginity. If that cannot be, a woman whose husband dies should stay a widow.
stances.quote: For the highest blessing, if any can possess it, is the grace of virginity, but if this cannot be, and it chance to a woman to lose her husband, let her remain a widow
stances.translation: Catena Aurea on St Luke, Oxford translation edited by John Henry Newman, 1843
stances.work: Homilies on Luke, Homily 17 (on Luke 2:36-38), as excerpted in Thomas Aquinas, Catena Aurea on Luke
stances.context: Origen's Homilies on Luke survive only in Jerome's Latin translation. This line reaches us through Aquinas's thirteenth-century anthology, which may shorten the text, so check against a Latin edition before relying on the exact words. Against Celsus 7.48 praises Christians "who maintain a perpetual virginity" for no human honour. Eusebius (Church History 6.8) says the young Origen castrated himself, taking Matthew 19:12 literally. Some of Origen's teachings were condemned long after his death (553), so treat him as partly heterodox.

stances.summary: Nothing compares with virginity. Those who put marriage on a level with it are fools, though marriage is excusable and fornication is not.
stances.quote: Blessed is such beauty and worthy of God; for nothing is to be compared with virginity. Thus, then, those who set marriage side by side with fornication grievously err; and those who think that marriage is to be placed on an equal footing with virginity are utterly wretched and foolish.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF second series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Martin's saying, told by his disciple Gallus in the dialogue by Sulpicius Severus (about 404), who knew Martin well. Martin read it from a meadow: grass grazed by cattle is marriage, ground rooted up by pigs is fornication, and the untouched flowering part is virginity. The saying ends: "marriage belongs to those things which may be excused, while virginity points to glory, and fornication must incur punishment unless its guilt is purged away through atonement." Orthodox.

stances.summary: Married life is a small, safe town where the weak are saved. It is not marvellous for virtue. The heights belong to the continent.
stances.quote: For they find as it were a little city, wherein to be protected from the fire; since this married life is not indeed marvellous for virtue, but yet is secure from punishment.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF second series vol. 12, 1895
stances.location: Book 3, chapter 27 (admonition 28, the married and the single)
stances.context: Written about 590. He reads Lot's flight from Sodom as a picture: "the height of the mountains is the purity of the continent", while the small town of Zoar is married life. He still says the single may marry "without blame, if only they have not vowed better things." Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: God does not command lifelong continence, since people must be born. But whoever can keep it wins an incomparable reward. It is the summit of all the virtues.
stances.quote: If anyone, He says, is able to do this, he will have an outstanding and incomparable reward. This kind of continence is, as it were, the summit and the completion of all the virtues.
stances.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin; the ANF translation (William Fletcher, vol. 7, 1886) left this chapter in Latin
stances.original: Si quis hoc, inquit, facere potuerit, habebit eximiam incomparabilemque mercedem. Quod continentiæ genus quasi fastigium est, omniumque consummatio virtutum.
stances.context: Written about 303-311. Earlier in the chapter he says God did not order continence as a binding law, because people must be born, but allows it. Lactantius was a teacher of rhetoric and later tutor to Constantine's son. Some of his ideas were idiosyncratic, but he was not condemned.

stances.summary: He points with pride to Christians who have kept themselves pure from childhood to old age, as proof of Christ's teaching.
stances.quote: And many, both men and women, who have been Christ's disciples from childhood, remain pure at the age of sixty or seventy years; and I boast that I could produce such from every race of men.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 155 to the emperor. Justin does not rank celibacy above marriage in so many words; he offers lifelong continence as evidence. Chapter 29: "whether we marry, it is only that we may bring up children; or whether we decline marriage, we live continently." Martyred about 165. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Many Christians grow old unmarried to live closer to God. Remaining a virgin brings a person nearer to God.
stances.quote: Nay, you would find many among us, both men and women, growing old unmarried, in hope of living in closer communion with God. But if the remaining in virginity and in the state of an eunuch brings nearer to God, while the indulgence of carnal thought and desire leads away from Him
stances.translation: B.P. Pratten, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written about 177 to Marcus Aurelius. The same chapter condemns second marriage (see claim b). Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Christ gave His Church two ways of life. The perfect way gives up marriage and property. The humbler way marries and works, with a second grade of piety.
stances.quote: Two ways of life were thus given by the law of Christ to His Church. The one is above nature, and beyond common human living; it admits not marriage, child-bearing, property nor the possession of wealth
stances.translation: W.J. Ferrar, SPCK, 1920
stances.context: Written about 314-318. A few lines later: "Such then is the perfect form of the Christian life. And the other more humble, more human, permits men to join in pure nuptials and to produce children... And a kind of secondary grade of piety is attributed to them" Eusebius, the church historian, leaned toward Arius before and after Nicaea, so his orthodoxy is disputed. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Those betrothed to Christ instead of a husband escape the curse laid on Eve and the pains of childbirth. They receive a name better than sons and daughters.
stances.quote: All those that are betrothed to Christ are far removed from the curse of the Law, and are redeemed from the condemnation of the daughters of Eve; for they are not wedded to men so as to receive the curses and come into the pains.
stances.translation: John Gwynn, NPNF second series vol. 13, 1898
stances.context: Aphrahat, known as the Persian Sage, wrote in Syriac inside the Persian Empire between 337 and 345. He addressed the sons of the covenant, celibate ascetics living inside the church. In section 4 he advises a celibate who cannot live apart from a woman to marry openly rather than fall. Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: An unmarried man in the world has his hands chained and can still run to the monastic life. A married man is bound hand and foot. Yet married people who live well are not far from the Kingdom.
stances.quote: For the unmarried man in the world, bound only by his affairs, is like one whose hands are in chains, and so whenever he wants to run to the monastic life, nothing stops him. But the married man is like one bound hand and foot.
stances.translation: Own close rendering of the Greek (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 88); the standard English translations (Moore 1959; Luibheid and Russell 1982) are copyrighted
stances.original: Ὁ γὰρ ἄγαμος ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ μόνοις τοῖς πράγμασι δεδεμένος, τῷ ἐν χερσὶ τὰ κλοιὰ περικειμένῳ ἔοικε (διὸ καὶ ὅτε βούλεται δραμεῖν πρὸς τὸν μονήρη βίον οὐ κωλύεται)· ὁ δὲ γήμας, τῷ ἐν χερσὶ καὶ ποσὶ τοὺς δεσμοὺς περικειμένῳ
stances.location: Step 1, section 36 in the Greek text at the url
stances.context: Written in the early seventh century by the abbot of Sinai, for monks. In the next section (37) married people ask how they can follow the monastic life. He answers with a short rule: do all the good you can, slander no one, steal from no one, lie to no one, do not miss church, be kind to the needy, keep to your own wives. In the Greek: "Ἐὰν οὕτως ποιήσητε, οὐ μακρὰν (641.) ἔσεσθε τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν", that is, if you do this, you will not be far from the kingdom of heaven (own rendering). He honours married faith but ranks the monastic life higher. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Celibacy is blessed for those given the gift, but it does not make a man. The one who serves God through wife, children and household, and stays faithful through all its trials, surpasses the single man.
stances.quote: one is not really shown to be a man in the choice of single life; but he surpasses men, who, disciplined by marriage, procreation of children, and care for the house, without pleasure or pain, in his solicitude for the house has been inseparable from God's love, and withstood all temptation arising through children, and wife, and domestics, and possessions.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written about 200. The next lines: the man with no family "is in a great degree free of temptation. Caring, then, for himself alone, he is surpassed by him who is inferior, as far as his own personal salvation is concerned, but who is superior in the conduct of life" (same page). Stromata book 3 defends marriage at length against groups who rejected it (ANF printed that book only in Latin). There, in chapter 1, he calls continence and those who have it from God blessed while admiring a single marriage; in chapter 12 he grants that continence chosen with reason earns greater dignity with God, and that marriage has its own services to the Lord. This is the strongest voice in the pool against ranking the single life above marriage, but it is a middle view, not a denial. Some later writers doubted his orthodoxy; he was never condemned.

stances.summary: Whoever can live in lifelong purity should do so for the Lord's honour, but must never boast of it or think himself above the bishop.
stances.quote: If any one can continue in a state of purity, to the honour of Him who is Lord of the flesh, let him so remain without boasting. If he begins to boast, he is undone; and if he reckon himself greater than the bishop, he is ruined.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 107-110 on the way to his martyrdom in Rome. In the same breath he tells husbands to love their wives "even as the Lord the Church" and asks that marriages be made "with the approval of the bishop". He honours celibacy but forbids treating it as a rank. Orthodox.

stances.summary: No state of life counts by itself, whether virgin, married, monk or layman. God looks at a person's desire and gives the Spirit to all.
stances.quote: Verily, virginity by itself is nothing, nor marriage, nor life as a monk, nor life in the world; for God seeketh the desire [of a man], and giveth the Spirit unto every man.
stances.translation: E.A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise, or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.location: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, book 2 (Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men), saying 4
stances.context: Macarius of Egypt (about 300-391), a founder of Scetis. A voice told him he had not yet reached the level of two women in a city. They were married to two brothers, had lived together twelve years without one quarrel, and had vowed never to speak a worldly word. They had wanted to join the virgins, but their husbands would not agree. The Greek alphabetical collection has the same story under Macarius the Great. The same Budge chapter tells of the married shepherd Eucharistos and his wife Mary, who outstripped two monks (though they lived in continence), and of Antony and a tailor in Alexandria. Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Once baptised, virgins, widows and married women have equal merit if their lives are otherwise equal. There is one reward in heaven for all who keep their baptism.
stances.quote: He says that virgins, widows, and married women, who have been once passed through the laver of Christ, if they are on a par in other respects, are of equal merit.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.location: Book 1, section 3 (Jerome's statement of Jovinian's first proposition)
stances.context: Jovinian was a monk in Rome who, about 390, wrote against ranking virginity above marriage. His books are lost; his words survive only as quoted and summarised by his opponent Jerome, so this is a hostile witness. His fourth proposition, in the same passage, is "that there is one reward in the kingdom of heaven for all who have kept their baptismal vow." He was condemned by Pope Siricius at Rome and by a synod under Ambrose at Milan (about 393). Jerome's Against Jovinian and Augustine's On the Good of Marriage and On Holy Virginity were written against him. Heterodox (condemned). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Marrying again after a spouse dies is no sin. Staying unmarried brings greater honour with the Lord.
stances.quote: There is no sin in marrying again, said he; but if they remain unmarried, they gain greater honour and glory with the Lord; but if they marry, they do not sin.
stances.translation: F. Crombie, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written in Rome in the first half of the second century. The angel of repentance answers Hermas's question about a widower or widow who marries. It is one of the earliest Christian rulings on the question after the New Testament. Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Second marriages are lawful and not to be condemned. He will not even condemn third or fourth marriages. But staying a widow is more blessed.
stances.quote: Wherefore this in the first place you ought to know, that by the good, which you have chosen, second marriages are not condemned, but are set in lower honor.
stances.translation: C.L. Cornish, NPNF first series vol. 3, 1887
stances.work: On the Good of Widowhood (De bono viduitatis)
stances.context: Written in 414 to the widow Juliana. In the same section he attacks Tertullian and the Montanists and Novatianists for treating second marriages as unlawful, "which the Apostle with sober mind allows to be altogether lawful." Section 15 on third and fourth marriages: "I dare neither to condemn any marriage, nor to take from these the shame of their great number." To every widow he says "you will be more blessed, if you shall have so continued." Orthodox.

stances.summary: Paul allows a second marriage as a concession to those who cannot contain themselves. It is no sin, but it falls short of the perfection of the gospel life.
stances.quote: And if the apostle, because of lack of self-control and burning, grants someone a second marriage by concession, this man too does not sin according to the covenant, since the law does not forbid it; but he does not fulfil the heightened perfection of the life lived by the gospel.
stances.translation: Own close rendering of the Greek (Dindorf 1869 edition, Stromata 3.12.82), checked against the Latin version printed in ANF vol. 2 (1885), which left book 3 untranslated
stances.original: et si cui Apostolus propter intemperantiam et ustionem, veniam secundi concedit matrimonii; nam hic quoque non peccat quidem ex Testamento (non est enim a lege prohibitus), non implet autem summam illam vitæ perfectionem, quæ agitur ex Evangelio.
stances.context: The "original" field gives the Latin version printed at the url, because ANF did not translate book 3 into English. The Greek (Dindorf edition, https://archive.org/stream/clementisalexand00dind/clementisalexand00dind_djvu.txt, poor OCR) reads in part "οὐ πληροῖ δὲ τῆς κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον πολιτείας τὴν κατ᾽ ἐπίτασιν τελειότητα". Clement goes on: the one who stays single after a spouse dies, keeping the union that death has ended undefiled, wins heavenly glory. Earlier, in 3.1, he says of second marriage only that Paul allows it to those who burn.

stances.summary: He does not forbid second marriages, but he does not advise them, and he disapproves of repeated ones. It is lawful to marry, but more fitting to abstain.
stances.quote: For I do not forbid second marriages, only I do not advise them. The consideration of human weakness is one thing, the grace of chastity is another. I say more, I do not forbid second, but do not approve of often repeated marriages, for not everything is expedient which is lawful
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF second series vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written about 377. The whole treatise was prompted by a widow in his diocese who was thinking of remarrying; Ambrose wrote partly so no one would think he had advised it. Chapter 15 argues against remarrying for the sake of children, pointing to stepfamily strife. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Second and even later marriages are not condemned in the Church, but they are not praised either. They are a relief for weakness, not a glory.
stances.quote: For my own part, I now once more freely proclaim that digamy is not condemned in the Church— no, nor yet trigamy — and that a woman may marry a fifth husband, or a sixth, or a greater number still just as lawfully as she may marry a second; but that, while such marriages are not condemned, neither are they commended.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.work: Letter 48, to Pammachius (defence of the books against Jovinian)
stances.context: Written about 394. The next sentence: "They are meant as alleviations of an unhappy lot, and in no way redound to the glory of continence." His tone elsewhere is much harsher. In Against Jovinian 1.14 he says of repeated marriages that it is "more tolerable for a woman to prostitute herself to one man than to many". Letter 54 (to the widow Furia) ends: "Think every day that you must die, and you will then never think of marrying again." Letter 123 (409) begs the young widow Ageruchia not to remarry and tells of a Roman woman who had had twenty-two husbands. He would never call remarriage "perfectly fine", but he refuses to call it a sin. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Paul allows a second marriage. Whether a person is a virgin or in a first or second marriage, all must pursue holiness to reach the Kingdom. Yet he urged widows to stay unmarried.
stances.quote: Therefore that we may be accounted worthy to see Him, whether we be in virginity or in the first marriage or the second, let us follow after this that we may obtain the kingdom of heaven
stances.translation: Talbot W. Chambers, NPNF first series vol. 12, 1889
stances.context: Earlier in the same section: "he allows even a second marriage, saying, only in the Lord." In his Letter to a Young Widow (NPNF first series vol. 9) he calls the name of widow "not a title of calamity but of honour" and tells how his own mother was widowed at about twenty and never remarried, to the loud admiration of his pagan teacher: "what women there are among the Christians." He also wrote a short treatise, On Not Marrying Again, urging widows not to remarry; its English versions are modern and copyrighted, so it is not quoted. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Someone married twice may be a much better person than someone married once. Yet Paul bars the twice-married from church office, and widows are urged to stay widows.
stances.quote: Now, when we saw that some who have been married twice may be much better than those who have been married once, we were perplexed why Paul does not at all permit those who have been twice married to be appointed to ecclesiastical dignities
stances.translation: John Patrick, ANF vol. 9, 1896
stances.work: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew
stances.context: Origen goes on to imagine a man widowed young who lived the rest of his life in perfect self-control, and asks why such a man should be passed over for a bishop who married once and lived with little discipline. He then gives a symbolic explanation of the rule. In his Homily 17 on Luke (see claim a) he urges a woman who loses her husband to remain a widow. That homily is widely reported to say more against second marriages, but its Latin text was not loaded here, so nothing more is claimed from it. Partly heterodox (some teachings condemned in 553).

stances.summary: Paul would rather widowed people stay single. He allows a second marriage as medicine for those sick with passion, not as a good in itself.
stances.quote: Thus also the apostle speaks here, first saying that he wished all were healthy and continent, as he also was, but afterwards allowing a second marriage to those who are burdened with the disease of the passions, lest they should be wholly defiled by fornication
stances.translation: William R. Clark, ANF vol. 6, 1886
stances.work: The Banquet of the Ten Virgins (Symposium)
stances.context: Just before, the speaker compares it to giving food during the Easter fast to someone dangerously ill, and says Paul allowed a second marriage "not as though he expressed the opinion that a second marriage was in itself" good (the New Advent page misprints "good" as "flood"). The words belong to the character Thalia in Methodius's dialogue. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: A first marriage is law, a second is an indulgence, a third is a transgression, and anything beyond is swinish.
stances.quote: The first is law, the second is indulgence, the third is transgression, and anything beyond this is swinish, such as has not even many examples of its wickedness.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached in Constantinople in 380. Just before: "I think that the Word here seems to deprecate second marriage. For, if there were two Christs, there may be two husbands or two wives; but if Christ is One, one Head of the Church, let there be also one flesh, and let a second be rejected". So he tolerates a second marriage as a concession while wishing it rejected. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Early view: after his death his wife should not remarry, for her own good. If a widow must remarry, she should at least marry a Christian.
stances.quote: The precept, therefore, which I give you is, that, with all the constancy you may, you do, after our departure, renounce nuptials; not that you will on that score confer any benefit on me, except in that you will profit yourself.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 200-206, before his Montanist period. Book 2 opens with "the next best advice, in regard of human infirmity": if a widow does remarry, she must "above all" marry in the Lord. So at this stage he discourages remarriage but treats it as allowed. He changed his mind later (next entry). Heterodox in his later years (Montanist).

stances.summary: Later view: a second marriage, even after a spouse has died, is a kind of fornication. Christians admit one marriage as they admit one God.
stances.quote: If we look deeply into his meanings, and interpret them, second marriage will have to be termed no other than a species of fornication.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 208-212, as he moved into Montanism, to a fellow Christian whose wife had just died. In On Monogamy (about 217, fully Montanist), chapter 1: "We admit one marriage, just as we do one God." He there claims the Paraclete now requires single marriage, and mocks the mainstream church as "Psychics" for allowing remarriage. This is a clear change of mind from To His Wife. Augustine later names Tertullian as the one who attacked second marriages "as though unlawful". Heterodox (Montanist).

stances.summary: A Christian should stay as born or marry once. A second marriage is disguised adultery, even if the first wife has died.
stances.quote: For he who deprives himself of his first wife, even though she be dead, is a cloaked adulterer, resisting the hand of God, because in the beginning God made one man and one woman
stances.translation: B.P. Pratten, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written about 177 to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. Just before: "a person should either remain as he was born, or be content with one marriage; for a second marriage is only a specious adultery." This is the bluntest early rejection of remarriage after death, and it comes from a mainstream apologist, not a sect. Not in the candidate pool. Orthodox.

stances.summary: A second marriage is not forbidden, but it carries a penance: a year or two away from communion. Third marriages are no longer marriage but "limited fornication".
stances.quote: In the case of trigamy and polygamy they laid down the same rule, in proportion, as in the case of digamy; namely one year for digamy (some authorities say two years); for trigamy men are separated for three and often for four years
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Letter 188, the first canonical letter to Amphilochius
stances.context: Written about 374. Basil reports the existing rules of earlier Fathers rather than inventing them. Letter 199, canon 24: "There is no special rule for a widower. The punishment appointed for digamy may suffice." Letter 217, canon 50: "There is no law as to trigamy... We look upon such things as the defilements of the Church. But we do not subject them to public condemnation, as being better than unrestrained fornication." He permits a second marriage, but treating it as something needing penance is a clear "no" to "perfectly fine". Orthodox.

stances.summary: For herself: there is only one marriage, as there is one birth and one death. Her promised husband was not dead but only away, alive in God, so she would stay faithful to him.
stances.quote: she would say that it was absurd and unlawful not to be faithful to the marriage that had been arranged for her by her father, but to be compelled to consider another; since in the nature of things there was but one marriage, as there is one birth and one death.
stances.translation: W.K. Lowther Clarke, The Life of St. Macrina, SPCK, 1916
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
stances.location: Section headed "Death of the young man" (Migne PG 46, col. 964C-D)
stances.context: Macrina was betrothed at twelve; the young man died before the wedding. She refused every later suitor. Her brother Gregory reports her words in indirect speech; he knew her all his life and was at her deathbed (379). He adds that she held the young man "to be absent only, not dead; it was wrong not to keep faith with the bridegroom who was away." She applied this to herself; there is no record of her condemning widows who remarried. She later led her mother and household into an ascetic community at Annisa. Orthodox.

splits_fathers: Claim a: almost no split. From the second century on, nearly every recorded voice ranks a life of virginity or continence given to God above marriage: 21 of the 25 stances found agree, across Latin, Greek and Syriac writers, bishops and monks, orthodox and schismatic. Almost all of them also defend marriage as good against groups that condemned it (Encratites, Marcionites, Manichees), so the typical view is that both are good and one is better. The real dissent is thin. Jovinian (condemned about 393) said virgins, widows and wives are of equal merit. Clement of Alexandria held a deliberate middle view in which the faithful householder surpasses the single man in the conduct of life. A desert saying of Macarius says no state of life counts by itself. Ignatius honours celibacy but forbids treating it as a rank. Within the candidate pool only Clement and Ignatius stand away from the majority, and only partly. Intensity varies a lot: Jerome and Martin of Tours (putting marriage 'on an equal footing with virginity' is foolish) at one end; Chrysostom ('the married but little below the unmarried') and Gregory of Nazianzus (virgins and wives, be one in the Lord) at the gentle end. Claim b: here the Fathers really split, but not at the point the claim names. No Father says remarriage is 'perfectly fine' without reserve, and nearly all say staying a widow is better. The live question was whether it is allowed at all. Lawful and no sin: Hermas, Augustine (he will not condemn even third or fourth marriages), and the councils of Nicaea and Laodicea against the rigorists. Lawful but a concession to weakness, to be discouraged: Clement, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, Origen, Methodius, Gregory of Nazianzus ('the second is indulgence'), and Tertullian in his early years. Wrong: Athenagoras ('a specious adultery'), Tertullian as a Montanist ('a species of fornication') and the Novatianists; Basil's canons impose a penance of a year or two. Macrina refused it for herself because 'there was but one marriage, as there is one birth and one death'. Every Father also accepted that a twice-married man could not be ordained.
splits_people_today: Claim a: today most people disagree. Secular people mostly see celibacy or marriage as a personal choice with neither higher, and many would find the ranking unkind to married people. Most Protestants follow the Reformers, who rejected the idea that vowed celibacy is a higher state (Augsburg Confession, articles 23 and 27). Catholic teaching still holds that consecrated virginity is in itself the more excellent state (Council of Trent, session 24, canon 10; Pius XII, Sacra Virginitas, 1954) while honouring marriage as a sacrament; the Catechism (1618-1620) presents the two as complementary. Orthodox Christians honour monasticism as the angelic life but rarely press a ranking on lay people. So this claim splits players well (a traditional Catholic or Orthodox minority agrees; most others disagree or say neither) but splits the Fathers poorly, since nearly every Father would answer agree. Claim b: today almost everyone agrees, Christians included. Catholic law allows remarriage after a spouse's death with no penalty. The Orthodox Church allows a second and third marriage but with a more penitential rite, and a widowed priest may not remarry and keep serving. A claim nearly everyone agrees with tells the quiz little about the player; the rare 'disagree' would match Athenagoras and the later Tertullian.

misattributions.line: He who too ardently loves his own wife is an adulterer.
misattributions.truth: Jerome quotes it in Against Jovinian 1.49 from 'Xystus in his Sentences' (the Sentences of Sextus, a collection of maxims), inside a long passage generally thought to draw on Seneca's lost treatise On Marriage. He endorses it, but it is not his coinage. NPNF wording: 'Hence Xystus in his Sentences tells us that He who too ardently loves his own wife is an adulterer.' https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/30091.htm

misattributions.line: The love of husband and wife is the force that welds society together.
misattributions.truth: Genuine thought from Homily 20 on Ephesians, but that wording comes from a modern, copyrighted translation. The public-domain NPNF (1889) reads: 'there is nothing which so welds our life together as the love of man and wife.' https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230120.htm

misattributions.line: Whoever denigrates marriage also diminishes the glory of virginity.
misattributions.truth: Genuine (On Virginity 10.1; quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1620), but the English is modern. No public-domain English of On Virginity was found, so quote it only as an own rendering of the Greek.

misattributions.line: All who, by human law, are twice married, are in the eye of our Master sinners.
misattributions.attributed_to: Justin Martyr, cited as condemning widows or widowers who remarry
misattributions.truth: Genuine line (First Apology 15), but it sits among Christ's sayings on divorce, directly after 'Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced from another husband, commits adultery.' It most likely means remarriage after divorce, which Roman law allowed. It is not clear evidence about remarriage after a spouse's death, so it was not used as a stance. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm

In Letter 188, canon 4, Basil uses 'limited fornication' for trigamy and polygamy (three or more marriages). For a second marriage he records only a penance of one year, or two by some authorities. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202188.htm

misattributions.line: Second marriage is a species of adultery.
misattributions.truth: 'Second Marriage a Species of Adultery' is the chapter heading in the ANF edition, supplied by the editor. Tertullian's own sentence says second marriage must be termed 'no other than a species of fornication'. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0405.htm

misattributions.line: The second marriage is a transgression.
misattributions.truth: A misquotation of Oration 37.8. He says: 'The first is law, the second is indulgence, the third is transgression.' The second marriage is tolerated; the third is the transgression.

misattributions.line: What is permitted is not good.
misattributions.attributed_to: Tertullian, quoted as a general moral rule
misattributions.truth: Genuine (To His Wife 1.3, written before his Montanist period), but it comes inside an analogy with fleeing persecution and is applied to marriage as a concession. It is not offered as a maxim about everything that is permitted.

misattributions.line: Marriage fills the earth, virginity fills heaven.
misattributions.truth: Genuine in substance. The NPNF wording (Against Jovinian 1.16) is 'Marriage replenishes the earth, virginity fills Paradise.'

misattributions.line: The popular wording beginning 'How beautiful, then, the marriage of two Christians'
misattributions.truth: Genuine passage (To His Wife 2.8), but that wording is from a modern, copyrighted translation. ANF (1885) reads: 'What kind of yoke is that of two believers, (partakers) of one hope, one desire, one discipline, one and the same service?' https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0404.htm

notes: 1. Framing. As worded, claim a splits players but not Fathers, and claim b splits Fathers but not players. Better disguised everyday statements: (i) 'Raising a family can be just as holy a life as a monk's or a nun's.' Agree: Clement (Stromata 7.12), Macarius, Jovinian; close to agree: Chrysostom ('but little below'). Disagree: Jerome, Martin, Gregory the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Athanasius. (ii) 'If my husband or wife died, I would want to stay single out of faithfulness to them.' Agree: Macrina, Tertullian, Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom (his mother's example), Origen. Neutral to disagree: Hermas and Augustine, who defend remarriage as lawful. Keep such items free of loading: many widowed people remarry for good reasons and should not feel judged. 2. Councils (corporate voices, not persons). Nicaea (325), canon 8, requires clergy coming over from the Novatianists to 'communicate with persons who have been twice married'. Laodicea (about 363), canon 1, gives communion 'by indulgence' to those who 'freely and lawfully joined in second marriages', after 'a short space' of prayer and fasting. Gangra (about 340), canons 9 and 10, condemn anyone who stays a virgin because he abhors marriage, and any virgin who 'shall treat arrogantly the married'. Pages: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3801.htm , https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3806.htm , https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3804.htm (NPNF second series vol. 14, Henry Percival, 1900). 3. The clergy rule is a separate question. Every Father accepted that a twice-married man could not be ordained (1 Timothy 3:2): Basil, Letter 188, canon 12, 'The canon absolutely excludes digamists from the ministry'; Origen, Commentary on Matthew 14.22; Jerome, Against Jovinian 1.14. Hippolytus (Refutation 9.7, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050109.htm) attacked Pope Callistus because under him 'bishops, priests, and deacons, who had been twice married, and thrice married, began to be allowed to retain their place among the clergy.' That is his only relevant line found, and it concerns clergy, so he gets no stance. 4. Pool figures with no stance found: Irenaeus (attacks the Encratites for rejecting marriage in Against Heresies 1.28.1 but does not rank the two; not quoted here); Perpetua (a young married mother; her Passion says nothing on this); Antony, Arsenius, Poemen, Moses the Black, Amma Syncletica, Evagrius, Isaac the Syrian, Benedict and Boethius (nothing found that compares celibacy with marriage; the monastic writers assume celibacy rather than argue it); Hilary of Poitiers (married, with a daughter; no public-domain text found); Ephrem (his Hymns on Virginity exist in English only in a modern, copyrighted translation; the Syriac was not searched; the NPNF hymns printed under his name say nothing direct); Pelagius (his Letter to Demetrias praises her virginity, but only modern English exists and the Latin was not loaded); Paulinus of Nola (he and his wife Therasia turned to a continent marriage, but his letters exist in English only in modern translation); John Cassian (Conference 21 tells approvingly how Abba Theonas left his unwilling wife for a monastery, but in chapter 10 Cassian says 'we not only in no way condemn marriage' and claims to give no opinion of his own; too hedged for a stance; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350821.htm). 5. Married figures worth knowing when writing the reveal: Tertullian wrote To His Wife to his own wife; Gregory of Nyssa writes On Virginity as a married man; Hilary and Perpetua were married; Chrysostom's mother was widowed at about twenty and never remarried; Macrina's betrothed died before the wedding. 6. Change of mind: Tertullian on claim b has two stances (early discouragement that still allows marriage to a Christian; later Montanist rejection). Jerome did not change his view, but in Letter 48 he defended it in milder terms after protests in Rome. 7. Evidence limits: Jovinian's words survive only in Jerome's hostile summary. Origen's Homily 17 on Luke survives in Jerome's Latin and is quoted here through the Catena Aurea; its passage on digamists is often reported as saying they are saved but not crowned, but that was not verified here, so it is not claimed. Martin's words come through his disciple Gallus in a dialogue by Sulpicius Severus. Macrina's words are her brother's report in indirect speech. Methodius speaks through characters in a dialogue. 8. Own renderings (Lactantius, Clement on claim b, John Climacus) are close literal translations made for this file. Their 'original' field holds the text exactly as printed at the url. For Clement that is the Latin version printed in ANF, since ANF left Stromata book 3 untranslated; the Greek is noted in context. 9. Capitals for God: quotations are exactly as the translators printed them; pronouns for God in these quotations are already capitalised where they occur, but recheck against the site rule when displaying. 10. Status: every stance was read in the source at its url with curl and copied by script from the raw page (whitespace collapsed). New Advent pages insert Bible references into the text (for example '1 Corinthians 7:38'); quotations were cut to avoid them.
